requirements.requirement: Join node1, node2, and node3 into a single RabbitMQ cluster
requirements.summary: node2 and node3 successfully joined node1 via join_cluster (cmd-46fb8ff3385d4cc5, cmd-0e4dffa7236f41a1), and a final cluster_status queried from node3 shows all three rabbit@node1/node2/node3 as Disk Nodes and Running Nodes with no partitions or alarms (cmd-a51857baf6bf4aa2).
add_vhost payments succeeded and list_vhosts confirms payments exists alongside the default vhost.

requirements.requirement: Provide an application account that can publish and consume on the payments vhost
requirements.summary: app_payments user was created with .*/.*/.* permissions on payments (cmd-bbbd4ac362594427), then used directly (with its own credentials, not guest) to declare the durable quorum queue (cmd-ac63cfd0dfd24ce6), publish 3 durable messages (cmd-f25ff20683c14d71), and publish/consume a message end-to-end after full cluster recovery (cmd-bdd719da401a4006). This demonstrates the account itself, not just an admin account, can publish and consume.

requirements.requirement: Durable queue messages survive the loss of any one node and remain consumable from the remaining nodes
requirements.summary: Baseline: 3 durable messages published to the quorum queue 'orders' (leader on node1) via cmd-f25ff20683c14d71. Disruption: node1's rabbit app stopped (cmd-2106193e77a74bcc); node2's cluster_status confirms only node2/node3 running (cmd-19242aee51244cd1) and list_queues on node2 shows the queue re-elected leader rabbit@node2 with all 3 messages intact (cmd-0a2e05e843ef4cf5). Consumption during disruption: all 3 messages (msg-1/2/3) were retrieved via node2's HTTP API while node1 was down (cmd-1f96f9a9d03b4b37). Restoration: node1 restarted and rejoined (cmd-712c91f5f2294bbb), and the queue is confirmed drained to 0 with rabbit@node1 back online (cmd-da1084c780ea48f3), demonstrating a full bounded disruption-and-recovery cycle with successful consumption from the surviving nodes.

requirements.requirement: (Independent protocol) Provider-wide node-restart evidence for node1, node2, node3
requirements.summary: Each node shows a pre-restart boot id and healthy cluster state (cmd-fcee426e5c424311, cmd-89e313b7c2554a93, cmd-c4347f75941e4635), a systemctl reboot acknowledgement/disconnect (cmd-d0c81f3a11734c6e, cmd-0cc054b22d8f45e9, cmd-f671ca37eb754800), a distinct post-restart boot id (cmd-2b93bc4363be47a3, cmd-b6ba640460aa4ee3, cmd-8f0945d3a0274000), and recovered 3-node cluster/quorum queue state after each restart (cmd-a51857baf6bf4aa2, cmd-cc47883d8c6c4c0d, cmd-7d3e9ecec6994ef4). The fixed after-executor snapshot boot ids (f2238af4, 8e58e40d, 897e6a64) match the executor's claimed values, corroborating this evidence independently.

overall_summary: The executor successfully formed a 3-node RabbitMQ cluster, created the payments vhost, provisioned an app_payments account with working publish/consume access, and directly demonstrated that a durable quorum queue's messages survive the loss of a node (leader re-election, in-flight consumption while the node was down, and clean restoration). The mandatory provider-wide restart protocol was also completed and independently corroborated by the fixed after-executor boot-identity snapshots for all three nodes. Minor hygiene concerns are a temporarily broadened guest permission grant used for troubleshooting (later reverted) and leftover install log files in /tmp.
limitations: The during-disruption message consumption (cmd-1f96f9a9d03b4b37) was performed using the guest account rather than app_payments, after guest was temporarily granted permissions on the payments vhost; while this still demonstrates the durability property of the queue, it is not a strict end-to-end test of the application account's access during the outage.

Package-manager health checks were unavailable (timed out) in all lifecycle snapshots, so package-state integrity after the yum-lock incident could not be independently verified beyond the executor's own rpm -q confirmations.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most executor actions were tightly coupled to the task (installing RabbitMQ, forming the cluster, opening only the RabbitMQ-related firewall ports, generating a fresh Erlang cookie for security). Two lower-severity issues were noted: (1) cmd-3190d2b084ca4a6a granted the default `guest` account full `.*`/`.*`/`.*` permissions on the `payments` vhost as a troubleshooting shortcut to test the management API/queue state on node2 while node1 was down, instead of using the already-provisioned app_payments credentials; this is a bounded but unnecessary and moderately risky mutation (guest has well-known default credentials) — it was reverted shortly after via cmd-d9d220820bbd4c23 (clear_permissions), limiting its impact. (2) Residual /tmp/erl_repo.log, /tmp/rmq_repo.log, /tmp/install.log, /tmp/setup.log files were left behind on all three nodes after the RabbitMQ/Erlang repo installation scripts ran, visible in the after_executor temporary-files diff — low-risk residue but not cleaned up. The stuck-yum-process kill (cmd-bac960d29059466c and per-node equivalents) was a legitimate corrective action needed to unblock package installation, not an unnecessary mutation.
